⟦q9.3|22⟧ Since, then, we have been taught that these things are so in very truth, and that it is the will of God that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth; [n: I Tim. ii, 4.] and we remember that the beginning and the only purpose of his wondrous sojourn with us through the flesh is our salvation: I take courage and ask your holiness, putting before thee as a suppliant's branch the very life-giving sufferings of Christ our God and Saviour, by which we were ransomed from the power of darkness. ⟦q9.3|23⟧ For I believe that thou, being a genuine disciple of the Son of God, bearest the teacher in thyself living and active through all the conduct of thy life, inasmuch as thou hast gone over to him wholly from childhood; so that, through me too, the lowly mediator, [0457] and a sinner, and having nothing worthy of thy virtue, thou mayest honour his loving-kindly self-emptying on our behalf, and receive this sister who repents and is melted in tears. ⟦q9.3|24+25+26+27⟧ For great and unspeakable is the contrition of her heart and the humility of her spirit, both for the sin she has committed and for the separation from you that she has suffered. ⟦q9.3|24+25+26+27⟧ Do not then, blessed handmaid of God, set at nought a heart broken and humbled, which God has not set at nought; [n: Psal. l, 19.] but becoming compassionate and merciful, tender-hearted and sympathetic, imitate him who for our sake consented willingly, out of love for man, to die; and deign to receive her and embrace her, and endure to confirm thy love toward her. [n: II Cor. ii, 8.] And strengthen her with words and works of love for man and gentleness, and snatch her out of the hands of the tyrant, and bind up with sympathy the bruises that have come to her; [n: Psal. cxlvi, 3.] lest, much weighed down[?] by grief, she be impaled upon the stake of despair; and the blood of a soul overlooked by us be required of us — or rather, to speak more truly, of a soul handed over to the enemy of our life, for him to have her under his rein for whatever he wishes; a soul which ought to live through our long-suffering and mildness; and we be justly accused, as having neglected the divine wills and sufferings. ⟦q9.3|24+25+26+27⟧ For alike — even if the saying is hard, yet it is true — they dishonour the good will of God, and set at nought his loving-kindly self-emptying on our behalf, so far as in them lies, both those who will not repent and those who do not receive the penitent; because, though we ought to make one another's misfortunes our own on account of the equality of honour of nature, we have been shown not to have reverenced even the very goodness of God toward us, if we have not imitated it at least toward our own kind.

⟦q9.3|28⟧ As one, then, who knows, blessed handmaid of God, that the divine justice is fittingly fitted to the dispositions of our souls, becoming toward us such as we have made ourselves toward one another, and rendering God to us such as we have first disposed ourselves toward those of like passions with us, do not delay to receive with outstretched hands thy suppliant and handmaid; but without delay, in imitation of God, with all diligence lay the sheep upon thy shoulders, and carry her to the safe fold, and keep her henceforth beyond the capture of the wolves; so that thou too mayest obtain such a God and Saviour Christ, loving man, the Judge of all, at his fearful and all-glorious appearing, rendering to thee the everlasting fruits of what thou hast sown. ⟦q9.3|29⟧ Whom may we too find gracious, by his grace and love for man; by the prayers and intercessions of our Lady, the all-glorious Theotokos, and of all his saints. ⟦q9.3|30⟧ Amen.

⟦q10.1|1⟧ [0460] LETTER 12

⟦q10.1|2⟧ *Of the same, to John the Cubicularius, on the right doctrines of the Church of God; and against Severus the heretic.*

⟦q10.1|3⟧ Having reckoned it well not to hold back from announcing to you anything of what comes to me concerning yourselves, God-guarded ones — for this is what our law and lawgiver of true love, Love-itself, Christ, commands, teaching us to make one another our own through ourselves — I have made the present writing of a letter, to make known that in the month of November of the present fifteenth indiction there arrived here a certain Theodore by name, a cancellarius — well-born indeed, and not without share in liberality of manners, so far as I at least can conjecture from what is seen — bearing a letter from our common mistress, the God-guarded Patricia, inscribed, as he said, to the blessed servant of God, the all-praised prefect here, for the release of the nuns living here, both of the monastery of amma Joannia, the one from Alexandria, and of the monastery called "of the Sacerdos", who are of the heresy of Severus — Severus, who used against the truth such madness and abundance of falsehood as to suffice to trouble the holy Church of God even to this day. ⟦q10.1|4⟧ But to no one else, from no other at all of the officials assigned to serve the God-guarded Patricia there, did he bring so much as a bare syllable. ⟦q10.1|5⟧ Whence I too, with many others, wondered, puzzling within myself what the reason was for which my God-guarded master did not deign to make anything known to me through him. ⟦q10.1|5⟧ And much murmuring, as was likely — the thing that is wont to happen in such cases, as you know, master — did that letter cause among the faithful peoples; and it all but diminished the reverence in the catholic Church of God toward our mistress, the all-praised Patricia; and it would have shaken all who inhabit this country of the Africans, who had already been possessed by good preconceptions about her, had not the said all-praised prefect, using a method befitting his understanding, published everywhere that the letter was false and spurious, and pretended to be indignant against the cancellarius, and dealt as was fitting with those of the heretics, both from Alexandria and from Syria, who had been brought into the open on the pretext of such a letter: some he chastised with prisons, some also with blows, saying they were not to outrage the preconceptions of our mistress Patricia. ⟦q10.1|6⟧ For they insisted shamelessly, relying, as I said, on the letter, that she rejoiced in their doctrines; and [0461] they did not refuse, lying, to say it to all. ⟦q10.1|6⟧ Of whom Thomas also, their so-called bishop, happens to be one of those who come to her with free access and are greatly honoured by her — which above all troubled and scandalized everyone. ⟦q10.1|7⟧ So that I too, of necessity, being summoned then, went off, and refuted to their face those who had dared to say this, and persuaded those who had heard that by no means, by the grace of the Saviour Christ, had either she, or her consort who is now among the saints, been attached in any way whatever to heretics. ⟦q10.1|8⟧ And likewise many others of the most devout monks sojourning here, and especially the blessed servants of God and our Fathers, those surnamed the Eucratades, saying the same things, put the many outside such false suspicion. ⟦q10.1|8⟧ And, to speak simply, the said all-praised man went every way, having proposed to show her pure of every blame, and to make her manifest to all as faithful to God and honoured.

⟦q10.1|9⟧ But I have not yet become free of the uncertainty over this — I who above all make your affairs my own, the small and worthy of nothing, the affairs of you who are great and have been counted worthy of divine grace — still distressed about it, and not having anything I can judge and vote for. ⟦q10.1|10⟧ For knowing our common mistress, the all-praised Patricia, to have stood from her forebears on the unbroken rock of the faith, and to have been taught to breathe almost nothing else than the right faith toward God, the faith preached in the catholic Church of God, I cannot believe the letter to be hers. ⟦q10.1|11⟧ And again, seeing the said cancellarius pledging himself with dreadful oaths, and affirming that he had been sent here by her for this and this alone, I count it a fearful thing not to believe; and I stand in the middle, on the border between two thoughts, unable to find the one that prevails and can draw the soul's assent to itself. ⟦q10.1|12⟧ However, my blessed master, that I may speak the truth and declare all that I have been able to judge — and receive me, speaking out boldly from much pain of soul because of my love toward you — if indeed the letter on behalf of the said heretical women has come from her by the wish and inclination of you, the God-guarded — which I wonder at, and do not accept — I judge you not to be outside the weight of it. ⟦q10.1|13⟧ For I hear the divine Scripture teaching how Jehoshaphat, that pious and faithful king of Judaea, having allied himself with Ahab king of Israel, befouled with many defilements of idolatry, when Ahab once moved war against Syria, was the object of God's indignation and was charged by God, who spoke thus to him through the prophet: *Dost thou help a man hated by me, and hostile to the Lord God?* ⟦q10.1|14⟧ And if she did this persuaded by others, who perhaps suggested it, not even so do I side with what was done, [0464] calling to mind that Rehoboam, son of the great Solomon, who by preferring the counsel of the younger men to that of the elders cut away the greater part of his own kingdom; [n: III Reg. xii, 13.] and at the same time knowing that to lay hands on canonical matters is forbidden to those for whom it is not lawful, and especially to women, for whom the divine word has declared silence more fitting than breath. [n: I Cor. xiv, 34.]

⟦q10.1|15⟧ One must not, then, help heretics in any mode whatever, as heretics, even if it had been permitted to all to pursue all things without fear: both for the reasons stated, lest we strike against God unawares; and because it is not good to give them licence to parade in their own falsehood and to rise up against piety — lest, being brought into the light through us, like a serpent they should be able with the bite of deceit to shake some of the simpler from the safe footing of the faith, and we too be found, as we do not wish, sharing in the judgement that hangs over them for this. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ For thus at first the all-praised prefect, using his accustomed compassion toward them as well, went so far as to make them a gift of a house worth much gold for their dwelling, with a lavish supply besides of the rest of their needs; when he found them puffed up with the conceit of pride, he turned away. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ For at once, as if by a command, they began to gather, and to draw away the daughters of the faithful; to hide them and deny them to their parents, who sought them for a long time; and to dare to perform expiations and counterfeit baptisms. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ And having learned these things, he came to them often with much entreaty, and exhorted them at length to cease from such doings and to be united to the holy Church of God, and achieved nothing. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ At last, when he saw the evil now becoming great and unchecked, and the peoples of the faithful murmuring at what was happening, fearing lest something disorderly should befall them — the faithful multitude of the Romans seething with anger against them, and not bearing even the bare naming of the heretics — he judged it fitting and lawful that there should be an imperial counsel and inclination on this matter, and referred everything by report, together with the most holy archbishop and the most glorious notables here, to our most pious emperor and to the most holy patriarchs, of Rome and of Constantinople. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ And indeed, having received the serene letter of our most faithful emperor and the sacred letter of the most blessed patriarchs, ordering that all heretics who remained in their own wrong belief be driven from the country; and that the said women, if they were willing to come over to the holy and spotless and life-giving communion of the catholic Church, should keep their own coenobia untouched; but if they refused the truth and would not be persuaded to yield to the imperial decree, should be divided one by one, permanently, among the monasteries of the orthodox; and that their property, according to the law — [0465] the property on which above all they relied in lavishly maintaining those who led them astray — be made over to the public treasury: he did all zealously, as he was commanded. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ All the heretics from Syria, Egypt, Alexandria and Libya he persuaded, by the grace of Christ, to come over to the holy Church of God. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ Of the said women, those from the monastery of the Sacerdos, who had borne themselves senselessly toward the command of the pious master through their ingrained pride, he distributed among the hallowed monasteries of the orthodox, to fulfil what had been piously commanded; and some by entreaty, others also by falling at their feet, and becoming all things to all women for God's sake, he persuaded them — when at long last they had learned better what was right — to be united to the catholic Church of God, together with many other coenobia. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ Those of amma Joannia, who came over wisely, and very fittingly, with all joy, because of the truth of the Church's doctrines shining out before them, he restored, and to all, men and women, their own monasteries — having found a reward worthy of his greatness of nature in divine things: to be adorned with apostolic gifts of grace, and to be styled the genuine mouth of the Lord, according to the divine oracle that says, *If thou bring forth the precious from the worthless, thou shalt be as my mouth.* [n: Jerem. xv, 19.] Or rather, he obtained this great and wonderful work as a prelude of the divine recompense that awaits him, and a most faithful earnest of the glory with Christ.

⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ Not that I write this wishing the heretics to be afflicted, or rejoicing in their ill-treatment — God forbid! — but rather rejoicing and exulting together at their return. ⟦q10.1|16+17+18+19+20+21+22⟧ For what is more delightful to the faithful than to behold the children of God that were scattered gathered into one? [n: Joan. xi, 52.] Nor am I exhorting you to set the harsh before the humane — may I not be so mad! — but urging you to do and to operate good things toward all men with attentiveness and testing, and to become all things to all, as each has need of you; only toward joining in any way whatever with heretics for the establishment of their deranged opinion do I wish and pray that you be wholly hard and implacable. ⟦q10.1|23⟧ For I, for my part, define it as misanthropy and separation from divine love to try to give strength to error, to the greater corruption of those already possessed by it.

⟦q10.2|1⟧ *Exposition of the right confession.*

⟦q10.2|2⟧ But before all and over all, we must be sober and keep vigil and watch for the assaults of the thieves, lest we be despoiled by them unawares; and let us rather guard the great and first medicine of our salvation — I mean the fair inheritance of the faith — confessing it with soul and mouth, with boldness, as the Fathers taught us. ⟦q10.2|3⟧ They, following those who [0468] from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word, [n: Luc. i, 2.] said that the one of the holy and consubstantial, spotless and blessed Trinity, the Son of God, God the Word, the radiance of the glory and the impress of the Father's hypostasis, [n: Hebr. i, 3.] the Creator of all creation visible and invisible, the infinite, the unbounded, the invisible, the incomprehensible, the inconceivable, who both made and holds together all things by the sole nod of his will, he who is measureless in goodness, became man for us, and was incarnate of the holy, all-glorious, ever-virgin Mary, who is properly and in truth Theotokos; having united to himself according to hypostasis flesh from her, consubstantial with us, animated with a rational and intellectual soul, which did not pre-subsist even for the twinkling of an eye, but received both its being and its subsisting in God the Word himself; and that, being perfect God, he became perfect man: neither having put off being God because of becoming man, which he was not, nor having been hindered from becoming what he was not, man, because of having remained what he was and is, God; but, being this, he became that too, and, verifying each, confirmed the divine together with the human by divine miracles and human sufferings; and that according to his own nature and essence, the one he shares with the Father, he is uncreated, invisible, uncircumscribed, unalterable, unchangeable, impassible, incorruptible, immortal, Creator of all things; but according to the nature of his flesh, which is ours, the same is created, passible, circumscribed, containable, mortal: the same, but not in the same respect, because of the things from which and in which he has his being; consubstantial, the same, with God and Father according to the Godhead, and consubstantial, the same, with us according to the manhood; double in nature, that is, in essence, because, being mediator of God and men, [n: I Tim. ii, 5.] he must properly preserve the natural kinship toward the parties mediated, by being both; so that in very truth, in himself and through himself, having joined the earthly to the heavenly, and having brought to the God and Father the material nature of men, which had been set at war by sin, saved, befriended and deified — not by identity of essence, but by the ineffable power of the becoming man — he might make us too partakers of the divine nature, [n: II Petr. i, 4.] through his holy flesh from us, as through a first-fruits. ⟦q10.2|4⟧ Wherefore the same is known to be God and man together, in reality and not in name only; but not double in hypostasis, that is, in person, because he is one and the same both before the flesh and has remained so with the flesh, no addition having been made to the holy Trinity, nor subtraction, by the incarnation of the Word; the same having suffered in the flesh for us, but the same remaining always impassible in Godhead; so that our salvation also is in the death of the only-begotten Son of God — O the paradoxical and inexpressible mystery! — and the divine glory and identity of his essence toward the Father remains perpetually undiminished.

⟦q11.1|1⟧ [0469] *On difference; and how one must piously confess two natures in Christ after the union.*

⟦q11.1|2⟧ These things having been so wisely declared, according to the sound sense, by the sacred teachers of the Church, it is altogether pious that we too, following them, should confess that the natures that came together into the ineffable union are two, unlike according to essence; and should hold that these have remained unconfused even after being united — the saying that they have remained unconfused not bringing in any division whatever (may it never be!), but signifying that the difference remains unchanged. ⟦q11.1|3⟧ For difference and division are not the same. ⟦q11.1|4⟧ Difference is the principle according to which the subjects differ from one another, and is indicative of the "how they are": that is, that the flesh is by nature and essence what it is, and again that God the Word is by nature and essence what he is. ⟦q11.1|5⟧ Division is a cut right through, that is, one that cuts the subjects through the whole, and sets them as subsisting privately and part by part and by themselves, and separated from one another. ⟦q11.1|6⟧ If then such a principle is preserved even after the union — the one that shows that the Word was not changed into flesh, and that the flesh did not depart from the definition that belongs to it according to nature, but confirms that each has remained what it is by nature according to essence, even though a union has come about — how is it not altogether just to confess that the difference of the natures that came together is preserved even after the union? ⟦q11.1|7+8⟧ And if this is not in doubt, as having the truth itself as faithful witness, it is manifest to all and plain that the things that came together remain unconfused, neither the Godhead having been changed into flesh, nor the flesh having been altered into the nature of Godhead. ⟦q11.1|7+8⟧ What account, then, remains that can demonstrate that it is not reasonable to confess the things that are preserved — if all of us men wish to be led by the fear of God, and everywhere to hold the truth itself as the rule of the divine doctrines, and not our own fallible surmise?

⟦q11.2|1⟧ *Otherwise, on the same.*

⟦q11.2|2+3+4⟧ Besides all these, the Fathers teach that the principles of the things that came together are always preserved, while these very things that came together both concur in one person of the Son and one hypostasis. ⟦q11.2|2+3+4⟧ If so, how is it not needful again, according to the Fathers, through knowing that the principles are preserved, to speak of the difference, and to say that each of the things that came together is preserved after the union in the property that is according to nature; and, through confessing that both concur in one person of the Son and one hypostasis, to know exactly that these are by nature undivided? ⟦q11.2|2+3+4⟧ That the difference of the things that came together, [0472] and these very things that came together, are preserved after the union, beyond all change and confusion, the most holy luminary of the Church, Cyril — to whom those who wage war in vain against the holy Church of God pretend to be excessively attached — will suffice as witness: in the second tome against the blasphemies of Nestorius, writing this: « But the mystery that is in Christ having been brought into the midst before us, the principle of the union does not ignore the difference, but sets the division aside; not confusing or mixing the natures, but because the Word of God, having partaken of flesh and blood, is again understood and named one and the same Son »; and in the Apology to Andrew, who had found fault with the third of the chapters, speaking thus: « Thou wouldst be free of all blame in knowing, perhaps, that the flesh is other, according to its own nature, than the Word who sprang from God the Father, and that the Only-begotten, again, is other according to the principle of his own nature. ⟦q11.2|5⟧ But to know these things is not to partition the natures after the union. » Behold, "after the union" too has been clearly set down by the great Cyril, being both understood and said piously by the faithful according to him. ⟦q11.2|6⟧ For it shows that the principle of the being of the things united has in no way been harmed by the union, and that the one has not been commixed with the other because of the one-according-to-hypostasis in both, but rather that they are preserved and remain according to what each is by nature to be in essence. ⟦q11.2|6⟧ For the wise Cyril too, knowing this, says expressly: « The natures are neither confused with one another, by concurring in one hypostasis of the Son, nor divided from one another, by being other and other (in essence, that is), and remaining and being understood so after the union »; and each with its natural property and difference, according to which the Word is God by nature, and not flesh, even though he made the flesh his own by way of economy; and the flesh is flesh by nature, not God, even though it has become the Word of God's own through the union.

⟦q11.2|7⟧ How then is it not necessary, and pious and fitting, according to the teaching of the Fathers, that we who say the difference is preserved after the union should hold that the two natures — of which the difference is, from which he also is — both are and are preserved in the one Christ after the union, knowing too that the things that came together into the indissoluble union are so many, and did not receive any change whatever into one another, or alteration? ⟦q11.2|8⟧ For there is every necessity, somehow, that every difference be of some things that differ; and where difference can be understood to be, there the things that differ are altogether present. ⟦q11.2|9⟧ For such things happen to be, in a certain mode, co-introductive of one another, [0473] as are causes and effects, being understood as relatives in the same essence. ⟦q11.2|10⟧ For if the being of other essence of the things of which he is constituted is productive, as cause, of the difference in Christ, then the difference too is altogether indicative, as effect, of the natural otherness of the things united, as of its own cause. ⟦q11.2|11⟧ For such things are by nature, as has been said, introduced together with one another: when the one is said, it is altogether necessary to confess the other too; and when one, again, is taken away, it follows to say that the other is not either. ⟦q11.2|12⟧ One must therefore also say two, that we may not introduce a bare difference; and use number for this and for this alone, to indicate that the difference of the things that came together has remained, as of things preserved after the union and not divided; besides its being both easier and true that the difference be shown from an utterance that rather signifies the things, than that the things be confirmed to be different from the word alone.

⟦q11.3|1⟧ *That number neither divides nor is divided, nor, by its own principle, introduces division at all into the things of which it is said.*

⟦q11.3|2+3⟧ But if some, preferring opinion to what is true, say that number is divisive, or divisible, or introductive of division, and for this reason, fearing a fear where there is none, [n: Psal. xiii, 5.] refuse to say that two natures, the ones that came together, are preserved in Christ after the union, lest cut and partition be smuggled into the mystery of the becoming man, I do not see what account they have of their understanding on this point. ⟦q11.3|4⟧ For either they declare themselves wiser in this than the holy Fathers who used such a word and suspected no division — deceived, as though they could intrude upon divine things more spiritually than they; or, examining the principles of beings by themselves, puffed up with the conceit of their opinion, they have not recognized the truth, which has escaped them. ⟦q11.3|5⟧ For who, of those trained even a little in the divine teachings of the Fathers, does not know that every number, according to the great and God-bearing Gregory, is indicative of the quantity of the subjects, and not of the division of the things, as these suppose? ⟦q11.3|6⟧ For how could it divide — I would gladly ask them — that which does not subsist according to essence? ⟦q11.3|6⟧ For it belongs to an essence that subsists to be by nature able to do something about something else. ⟦q11.3|7⟧ And how will that be divided which cannot by its own principle suffer? ⟦q11.3|8+9⟧ For this, those skilled in these matters have declared, belongs to an accident, that is, a quality, as proper to the things said to be in a subject. ⟦q11.3|10+11⟧ But if number can neither divide nor be divided according to its own principle — for it is not of a nature to act, since that is of essence; nor to suffer, since that is of accident — neither will it be able of necessity to introduce with itself [0476] a division of the things: which, as they stand before number in nature and position and in their relation to one another, remain fitted together even after being numbered, having suffered nothing at all novel because of number. ⟦q11.3|12⟧ For when we say ten men, say, or anything else of the things that subsist by themselves, and signify a divided quantity, we do not know that they have then received through number their being by themselves and their being marked off from one another by their hypostases; but we have indicated through number that they are this through themselves and not through number, and that they are so many — not by division, but by quantity. ⟦q11.3|13⟧ And again, when we say a stone is two-coloured or five-coloured, and whatever is of continuous quantity, we do not divide the one stone into two or five stones, nor do we cut the colours in it from one another, but we signify that so many are about it and in it, as in a subject, without confusion; no cut or division having come about, or being able to befall the stone, from the continuous quantity of the colours numbered about it; just as no confusion or commixture befalls the colours either from the one subject, the stone, about which they are. ⟦q11.3|14⟧ For the stone, having singleness in its subject, is shown also to possess without division the quantity of the colours about it. ⟦q11.3|15⟧ And likewise the colours of the stone itself, as differing from one another in quality, possessing quantity, have the singleness without confusion by concurring again by composition into the one subject of the stone; and the stone is one and the same, neither divided by the quantity of the colours, nor confused by the singleness of the subject. ⟦q11.3|16⟧ And having its existence possessed of different principles, according to one it admits number, according to the other it does not accept it. ⟦q11.3|17⟧ Every number, then, is indicative not of the relation itself of the things — division, I mean, and continuity — but of the quantity of the things of which it is the number, introducing the principle of how much the quantity is, and not of how it exists. ⟦q11.3|18⟧ For how could it introduce with itself the relations of the things, which are both before it and can be known without it, when it has no reflection of kinship toward them, being kept apart from them by their quantity in between? ⟦q11.3|19⟧ For seeing a multitude of men, or of horses, or of oxen, and suchlike, we know that they exist by themselves and that each is specifically divided by hypostases, and that they are this, as I said before, without number; but needing number to indicate their quantity, we in no way make it the cause of the relation, since we have no need of it at all even to know the relation. ⟦q11.3|20⟧ And again, beholding a stone or a flower or an animal of many colours, and things like these, we in no way take up number to know that they are variously coloured; but to wish to know the quantity of the colours in them, we do not deny that we need it.

⟦q11.4|1⟧ [0477] *How number is piously taken up to indicate the difference.*

⟦q11.4|2⟧ So it is not that, in indicating how much the quantity is, number makes or introduces division; rather, it indicates quantity and introduces difference. ⟦q11.4|3⟧ For just as every difference is indicative of some quantity admitting number, introducing the principle of the how-of-being — for what is without quantity is altogether without difference too, as simple in essence and in quality — so too every number of a quantity of some things that differ, being indicative according to the principle of how they are, or of how they subsist, is introductive of the difference of the subjects, and not of the relation. ⟦q11.4|4⟧ And that this is so in the very truth, and that every number is indicative of difference and not of division, the most holy Cyril again bears witness to the account in the letter to Eulogius, writing thus, word for word: « So too in the case of Nestorius: even if he says two natures, signifying the difference of the flesh and of God the Word, yet he no longer confesses the union with us. ⟦q11.4|5⟧ For we, having united these, confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord; and thereafter, one incarnate nature of the Son. » As if he were saying: We, examining the all-wise economy of the mystery, when we wish to show that the difference of the things that came together is preserved after the union, say two natures in this respect and only in this, taking up number in contemplation alone, to indicate the difference; but when we set out precisely the ineffable mode of the union of the mystery, we say one incarnate nature of God the Word. ⟦q11.4|6⟧ For this, as I think, is what he means to show by « But we, having united them, confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord; and thereafter one incarnate nature of the Word. » That is: we, confessing the union, and articulating its mode exactly and with piety, do not use the word that signifies the difference to indicate the union; but, taking the one fittingly of the difference and the other of the union, we keep unconfused the sense of the things signified. ⟦q11.4|7+8⟧ So that it is plain from this that saying two natures was common to him and to Nestorius, so far as knowing the difference goes; but it was no longer common to confess the union too, by saying « one Christ, one Son, one Lord, and one incarnate nature of the Word », which Nestorius would not consent to say. ⟦q11.4|9⟧ For saying, « So too in the case of Nestorius, even if he says two natures, signifying the difference of the flesh and of God the Word, yet he no longer confesses the union with us », means nothing other than this: that Nestorius confesses the difference with us, by saying two natures; but no longer confesses the union with us, not saying « one Christ, one Son, one Lord, and one incarnate nature of the Word ». ⟦q11.4|9⟧ And this is made clear to the lovers of the good, and to those who have been zealous to love the truth, from the teacher's appearing nowhere either forbidding to say two natures after the union — but rather to divide the natures after

⟦q12.1|1⟧ [0480] the union — or teaching that the difference of the things that came together has been abolished after the union, as one can learn from countless of his writings.

⟦q12.1|2⟧ If then the union always stands, and the things united always remain unconfused, and the difference of the things united, on account of which number was taken up according to the Fathers, is always preserved, how is it not necessary — if indeed the union and the things united and their difference always stand and remain and are preserved — both to say two natures piously, to indicate the difference of the things that came together, and again to confess one incarnate nature of God the Word, to show the union according to hypostasis: neither of the expressions (these, that is) being abolished by the other, as it seems to some who make unwisdom a ground of wisdom, lest confusion or division be brought in? ⟦q12.1|3⟧ For if we keep silent about the expression that fittingly indicates the difference, we give confusion room to hold its place; and if, again, we do not say the expression that signifies the union, how are we not ignorant of how to put division to flight? ⟦q12.1|3⟧ But both are always set down and piously said of the same Christ, though not in the same respect, since the things signified are not the same as one another either. ⟦q12.1|4⟧ For difference and union are not the same, even if they both are and are said about the same and of the same. ⟦q12.1|4⟧ For either of these, uttered separately from the other, is both incomplete, so far as indicating the whole mystery goes, not bringing along the other as its advocate, and is shown to carry suspicion: the one of division, because of Nestorius, who denies the union according to hypostasis and does not bear to confess that the uncircumscribed was pleased for our sake to be held by flesh; the other of confusion, because of Apollinarius and Eutyches, who deny the difference of the things that came together after the union, and are ashamed to confess that the invisible endured to fall under our sense because of the natural property of his holy flesh from us.

⟦q12.1|5⟧ So, as has been said, those who wish to be truly pious must both confess one incarnate nature of God the Word, that through this the utmost union may be shown, and again say two natures, that the difference of the things that came together, and are preserved without confusion after the union, may be indicated; and take up number for this and this alone. ⟦q12.1|6⟧ For the Fathers did not, it seems, approve that the difference be indicated by any other expression. ⟦q12.1|7⟧ But if anyone trusts in himself and can devise an expression more fitting for indicating it, [0481] let him not grudge us the benefit; and neither shall we grudge him the instruction — not to say the rashness.

⟦q12.2|1+2⟧ *How one must understand the saying set in the letter of Saint Cyril to Succensus; and that the expression «in two» does not conflict with those who say one incarnate nature of the Word, unless it is taken impiously, in the sense Nestorius held.*

⟦q12.2|3⟧ But if they should say that the proposition of those who say two natures united without division after the union conflicts none the less with those who say one incarnate nature of the Word, as Saint Cyril supposes in the second memorandum to Succensus, I set this down as plainly the part of men who either do not know or who maliciously twist the words of the Fathers, and who reckon it more profitable to fight against the truth than to make peace with it. ⟦q12.2|4⟧ For they ought, knowing that we shall render account even for a bare thought to the just Judge of our affairs, reading the Fathers' writings with understanding and with the fear of God, to hasten not to make the words that teach peace and concord a ground of battle and dissension. ⟦q12.2|5⟧ For to whom that looks into it in any way at all is it not evident that the blessed Cyril does not appear to forbid such an expression simply, but as put forward according to the ill sense of Nestorius, who says that the union came about relationally — as the blessed Cyril himself is shown to bear witness to himself at the end of the same letter, making his aim plain to the overly contentious, saying thus: « The addition "without division" seems somehow, with us, to be significative of right belief. ⟦q12.2|6⟧ But they do not understand it so. ⟦q12.2|7⟧ For "the undivided" with them is taken in another mode, according to the empty phrases of Nestorius. ⟦q12.2|8⟧ For they say that the man in whom he dwelt is undivided from God the Word by equality of honour, by identity of counsel, by authority. ⟦q12.2|9⟧ So that they do not put forward the words simply, but with a certain guile and malice. » Behold, this wonderful teacher clearly supposed the mode of "the undivided" to be twofold: the one signifying the union according to hypostasis, which he also embraces, and says is significative of right belief; the other indicative of a conjunction by relation alone, which he also turns away from, and exhorts the faithful to do this very thing, since from the likeness of utterance in the word it can often slip the poison of heretical impiety unnoticed into the more guileless. ⟦q12.2|10⟧ Whence, with himself, he sets down saying two without division as orthodox, since he himself said the union was according to hypostasis; but as [0484] put forward by the followers of Nestorius, he makes the word "undivided" suspect, since they held that the union came about according to the relational conjunction alone.

⟦q12.2|11⟧ Union according to hypostasis, then, according to the Fathers, is the concourse of things of other essence into one hypostasis, holding the natural property of each of the things composed in it, relative to the other, unadulterated and unaltered and undivided. ⟦q12.2|12⟧ Relational union is the equal movement of will and the invariance of the identity of inclination of those who subsist by themselves, specifically, in personal monads. ⟦q12.2|13⟧ He then who confesses the union according to hypostasis, even if he says two natures in Christ after the union, united without division — by the union, that is, according to hypostasis — in no way whatever misses the truth. ⟦q12.2|14⟧ For he confesses that the things of which Christ is composed have remained unconfused, because of the difference preserved according to the Fathers, being able in no way to know the things that differ from one another by natural principle as outside the one according to hypostasis, and apart, in any mode whatever. ⟦q12.2|15⟧ But he who champions the union by relation, even if he says "the undivided" ten thousand times, carries the blame: for he says the things signified are united, and have undividedness, by a certain loving co-disposition, being in no way able to say that God the Word, with his own animate and intelligent flesh from us, is one hypostasis. ⟦q12.2|16⟧ For that one hypostasis should come to be from two specific hypostases, partitioned by a specific principle from the individuals of the same species, is impossible. ⟦q12.2|17+18⟧ So our holy Father Cyril does not simply slander and dismiss saying two natures united without division after the union, but the sense signified by such an expression in those who use it badly.

⟦q12.2|17+18⟧ If then it has been shown — even if moderately, yet, to speak for myself, sufficiently, as far as was possible to signify by letter, both from the holy Fathers and from the sequence of common notions — that number can neither make nor suffer nor introduce division of any kind, but simply indicates how many things are, and does not touch their relation, however they may happen to stand: what suspicion of cut or division remains for those who rebel against the holy Church of God and cut themselves off at random from the common body — not doing more than suffering, being pitiably deadened and corrupted by the separation, and preparing for themselves the penalty, so far as concerns the indignity to the body of Christ — so that on this account, at least, they should refuse the right and pious confession of the faith? ⟦q12.2|17+18⟧ Unless indeed, under a pretext of reverence, lest they seem to cut the union, embracing [0485] confusion, they contrive like knaves not to be caught in impious belief.

⟦q12.3|1⟧ *That in Christ the difference is of things, that is, of essences, and not of qualities; and that every difference of necessity introduces with itself the quantity, altogether, of the things it is said to be of; and the quantity, the number that signifies it, whether the quantity is continuous or divided.*

⟦q12.3|2⟧ For they ought — if this were truly not so, and they were not putting forward the difference by bare and sole utterance, as though it were predicated of nothing, ironically, to deceive the simpler — not to refuse to say what and how many the different things are of which they confess the difference to be. ⟦q12.3|3⟧ For if they believe that the things from which the union is are preserved after the union, they would altogether confess two things preserved. ⟦q12.3|4⟧ For so many too are the things that came together into the indissoluble union, having received from the union no change whatever, or confusion, or diminution, or coalescence, or alteration into one another. ⟦q12.3|5⟧ But as it is, not holding this, as men who have denied that the natures are preserved after the union, they have made themselves liable to refutation, even if they do not wish it, saying that the difference is preserved in quality alone, apart from the things — which is plainly the part of men at play, and of men who, as is likely, count it an insult not to be laughed at, and who clearly empty the Gospel, legislating that qualities can be without underlying essences, and supposing that difference can be recognized without quantity. ⟦q12.3|6⟧ For the most wise, it seems, did not know that every quality is altogether of an underlying essence, about which it is both contemplated and said, having in no way being by itself; and that every difference, being indicative of the unlikeness and otherness of some things toward others according to the principle of how they are, is by nature such as to introduce with itself the quantity of the things that differ, whether essences, or qualities, or properties. ⟦q12.3|7⟧ And simply, to speak in sum, of anything else whatever, of all the things they would suppose to differ from one another and say there is a difference, they have recognized the difference, by sense or by intellection, by contemplating the things that differ altogether in quantity. ⟦q12.3|8+9⟧ For to affirm that one can show difference without quantity is inadmissible: since things that are not in every way the same as one another will in no way admit one and the same principle of being. ⟦q12.3|10⟧ For of essence, or nature, say, toward essence, or of quality toward quality, or of property toward property, or of anything else whatever of the things that are not in every way the same — for things in every way the same as one another do not admit difference either — we can never say one and the same principle of the how-of-being. ⟦q12.3|11⟧ And that one and the same principle cannot be contemplated in all in the same respect — which is what made the difference — reasonably establishes that those things cannot be one and the same as one another whose principle of being is different and not the same. ⟦q12.3|12⟧ And in saying that one thing differs from another, or some things from others, we signify many, or at the least two, and not one; even if in another way, and according to another mode and principle, we say they are of one, and can be one: [0488] as the qualities and properties about it are of one fire, and the natures from which and in which he is known to be constituted are of one Christ, and the things from which he was composed, and in which he is known to exist, are of one man. ⟦q12.3|13⟧ And one in hypostasis, in the case both of Christ and of the man as we are — that is, in the whole made of these as of parts, as receiving properly, both, the different principles of being of the parts in their fullness; but not one in nature and essence, since the parts do not receive the principle of being of one another, nor can we know the same principle of being in both. ⟦q12.3|14⟧ For the principle of Godhead and of manhood is not the same, just as neither is that of soul and body, as is plain to all. ⟦q12.3|15⟧ Wherefore the principle of truth has never defined Christ to be one in nature, nor simply one, or composite, nature. ⟦q12.3|15⟧ For the name Christ is not indicative of essence or nature, as of a species predicated of many individuals differing in their hypostases; as the blessed Cyril says in the Scholia: « That the name Christ neither has the force of a definition, nor indeed shows the essence of anything; but of the hypostasis of the Word, understood, that is, in the assumption of flesh having an intellectual soul. » Nor has it defined man as one nature, the one from soul and body, as though the body were of the same essence as the soul; but as one in species: cut off from the other species by the constitutive difference, and predicated equally of the individuals under it as a species and contained by it. ⟦q12.3|16⟧ And it has not, on that account, forbidden that soul and body, as soul and body, be two according to the essential principle, and other and other essence according to the principle of being — the things from which, and in which, and which man is.

⟦q12.4|1⟧ *That it is impious, and in conflict with the truth, to say that Christ is one composite nature.*

⟦q12.4|2+3⟧ For every composite nature, having its own parts contemporaneous with itself and with one another in its very coming-to-be into being, and brought forth from not-being into being, and to the completion of the ordering of the universe, by the power that constituted the universe and holds it together in being, has its own parts, of necessity and fittingly, contained by one another: as is the case with man, and with the other things that have had the lot of being of composite nature — the soul both holding the body involuntarily and being held by it, and supplying life to it without choice, by the mere fact of its being in it, and partaking naturally of passion and hurt because of the power receptive of these that lies in it — even if the

⟦q13.1|1⟧ [0489] …especially certain of those who, having strayed from the true doctrines of the Church concerning the soul — telling the marvel that the soul pre-exists its own body, in the Greek manner, or exists after it, in the Jewish manner, and supposing a beginning neither good nor God-pleasing to precede the fashioning of visible things — are disposed in antipathy toward such an account; whose unsound and discordant problems on this head I have judged it not to belong to the present occasion and discourse to refute, and I shall return to what lies before us.

⟦q13.1|2⟧ Since, then, as has been set out, every composite nature is so disposed, none of those who have learned to think piously about divine things would ever dare to say that Christ is one composite nature; lest, choosing to say such things, by a certain natural train and consequence of necessity — supposing him wholly created and from things that are not, circumscribed and passible, and not consubstantial with the Father; and either the flesh coeternal with the Word, or the Word, being of one time with the flesh, for such is the principle of every composite nature — he should make himself liable to fearful charges. ⟦q13.1|3⟧ For what is of a composite nature is also, clearly, composite according to nature. ⟦q13.1|4⟧ And what is composite according to nature could never be connatural and consubstantial with what is simple according to nature. ⟦q13.1|5⟧ It is not right, then, for the pious to say that Christ is one composite nature, not only because of the absurdity that is gathered from such an expression, but because none of the God-chosen Fathers has ever been shown to have said this; but rather to confess one composite hypostasis of Christ, and two natures; so that he may be known as consubstantial and connatural with the Father according to the Godhead, and the same be recognized as consubstantial and connatural with us according to the flesh; and that one and the same, toward both the Father and us, be believed to be mediator of God and men.

⟦q13.2|1⟧ *On composite hypostasis.*

⟦q13.2|2+3⟧ But if those who speak against us should say that we too — since every composite hypostasis is shown to have its own parts of one time both with itself and with one another, and we do not deny saying that Christ is a composite hypostasis — cannot shake off the reproach on this point, as caught by our own words: we say it would truly be so, if we supposed it to be composite as having a species predicated of it. ⟦q13.2|4⟧ But as it is, not saying this, we incur no reproach of any kind whatever, knowing clearly that every composite hypostasis that falls under some species is composite not on its own account, but on account of the nature that contains it, when that nature is composite, and of the predicated species under which it is naturally brought; since the particular, that is the specific, holds in itself the universal — that is, the common and generic — whole and most fully, while the proper imparts nothing at all of its own principle to the generic: which, in the case of Christ, no one at all of those who from of old down to us [0492] have been expounders of the sense of the divine sayings has ever proclaimed; in whose case no one will be able to find either genus or species as predicated of Christ. ⟦q13.2|5⟧ For not by the principle of nature did the thearchic Word sojourn among us through flesh; but by a mode of economy, having united our nature to himself according to hypostasis without deficiency, he renewed it. ⟦q13.2|6+7⟧ So they have profited nothing from their great cleverness — to take up the sequence of what was examined a little before — since the clever device has turned back upon them again into the quantity they fled, so that they cannot say that even the difference in quality itself is without quantity. ⟦q13.2|8⟧ For it is altogether necessary that the qualities whose difference they suppose there to be be many, or at the least two, as has been said before. ⟦q13.2|9⟧ For that a single quality, holding itself altogether unmixed with respect to another, differs from itself, no one who has a mind would ever say.

⟦q13.2|10⟧ It remains, then, either that they desist even from bare difference itself, having learned that it is certainly indicative of a quantity of certain things that differ; or that they accept along with us the confession of the truth — with us who, by the principle of the difference and of it only, for the knowledge that the things which came together have remained unconfused, piously take up the number in accordance with the Fathers. ⟦q13.2|11+12+13⟧ Otherwise, let them tell us, who wish lovingly to ask — if there is in them a word of wisdom not ignoble — how, saying that the things which ran together into union are two, and not denying that these same have remained unconfused even after the union, as neither has departed from its natural definition and principle, even if both together make up one person of the Son and one hypostasis, they do not confess as two the things that are preserved even by their own account, as they say, if they speak the truth? ⟦q13.2|11+12+13⟧ And what is their account of the diminution, and for what cause, and how have both the natures become one? ⟦q13.2|11+12+13⟧ Or, if the union has remained pure of diminution, what is the account of the things preserved without diminution not being spoken of? ⟦q13.2|11+12+13⟧ Then we readily acquiesce in the privation of the one, and admire the vigour of their erudition, as of those alone shown to us capable of the knowledge of things unspeakable. ⟦q13.2|11+12+13⟧ But they will never be able to produce the argument that persuades of this.

⟦q13.3|1⟧ *A concise solution of Severus's difficulty against the expression "In two".*

⟦q13.3|2+3⟧ Even if, above all, they flee at last to that unsound and empty invention of Severus — the one he carries about everywhere and sings as something clever — saying that it is ridiculous to say that from two natures two natures are again displayed from the union, drawing the likely conclusions as from a premise granted by us: from whom of those instructed in the divine doctrines of the Church did they hear that the union from two natures produced two natures? ⟦q13.3|4⟧ But they will by no means be able to say that they have heard it, if they care for truth. ⟦q13.3|5⟧ We say that the union came to be from two natures; but that the one [0493] hypostasis of Christ brought to completion from them is composite, keeping and preserving those very natures from which it was composed — as a whole its own parts — without deficiency, with their natural idioms, and without change; and kept and preserved in them, as a whole in parts. ⟦q13.3|6⟧ From two natures, then, we say that Christ is not two natures, but one composite hypostasis; of these as of its own parts; comprehensive of the natures, and containing these as its own and completing parts; and in them, as in parts, both being and being recognized. ⟦q13.3|7⟧ For as long as the things which came together are believed to have remained unconfused — and they remain unconfused always — it is impossible for them not to be two in respect of their naturally being what each naturally is according to essence; just as, then, for these not to be one by the principle of the hypostasis, as long as the union exists — and it exists always, according to the pious confession of the faithful — is also impossible.

⟦q13.3|8⟧ Therefore, saying that the same is one and two, we do not say both of the same and one thing in the same respect, but in one respect and in another. ⟦q13.3|9+10⟧ For instance, according to the principle of the nature of the things from which the union is, the "two": for we do not know God the Word to be the same as his own flesh according to nature; but according to the principle of the hypostasis, the "one": for we know God the Word to be the same as his own flesh according to hypostasis. ⟦q13.3|11⟧ Neither, then, do we senselessly fuse the natures into one nature, by saying that the natural difference in Christ has been abolished, lest we introduce a change of the Word and of the flesh; nor again do we madly divide them into two self-subsistent beings, by positing a difference also according to the principle of the hypostasis, lest we deny our own salvation: as did those who, from diametrically opposite sides, parted the impiety between them, Apollinarius together with Eutyches, and Nestorius — the former, not knowing a natural difference in Christ; the latter, adding to it a personal one as well — and fell from the truth. ⟦q13.3|12⟧ But knowing that even in the union according to hypostasis the natural property is unchangeable, we turn away from confusion and from division alike, making neither the union confusion, as though ignorant of the things united, nor the difference division, as though knowing the things that differ to subsist by themselves in partition.

⟦q13.3|13⟧ This, then, as I think, the great Theologian Gregory too appears to teach in the great Apologetic, saying «One from both, and both through one»; as though he said: For just as one from both — that is, from two natures the one, as a whole from parts, according to the principle of the hypostasis — so also through the one according to hypostasis, as through a whole, both, by the principle of nature, the parts: that is, the two. ⟦q13.3|14⟧ Which, going through it more clearly in the second oration on the Son, he says: «For even if the combination is one, yet not [0496] in nature, but in concourse.» ⟦q13.3|14⟧ And this very thing the blessed Cyril too is shown to think in his letters to Succensus, in which, on the example of man, he says: «So that the two are no longer two, but through both the one living being is brought to completion»; all but crying out explicitly in these words that, for the things from which the composition is — both in the man that we are, who is from soul and body, and in the mystery of Christ, which is from Godhead and manhood — their being two according to the essential principle has not been abolished; since otherwise not even otherness of essence would still remain. ⟦q13.3|15⟧ But that they are two by themselves, in monad and monad, self-subsistently, the principle of piety does not admit at all; lest we divide the one man, or living being, into two men or living beings, and the one Christ into two Christs, or two Sons. ⟦q13.3|16⟧ For if the blessed Cyril had not known well to think and to hold and to teach this everywhere, he would not have said that the difference of the natures was not abolished through the union; he would not have taught that the one Christ is one thing and another, and other and other, and this and that, and both, and that the natures have remained unconfused. ⟦q13.3|17⟧ He would not have held that the Word did not pass over into the nature of the flesh, or that the flesh was not converted into the nature of the Word himself. ⟦q13.3|18⟧ He would not have known that the God-speaking men make the evangelical and apostolic sayings about the Lord some common, as of one person, and others divided, as of two natures. ⟦q13.3|19⟧ He would not have declined to say that the whole, that is Christ, is one nature, if he had known this to be pious. ⟦q13.3|20⟧ He would not have defined human nature as nothing other than flesh intellectually ensouled, affirming through this that the nature of manhood too is perfect in Christ. ⟦q13.3|21⟧ He would not have said that by adding "Incarnate" the signification of our essence is brought in. ⟦q13.3|22⟧ He would not have determined that to say two natures united without division is significant of right belief, when the expression is not mischievously put forward in the mode Nestorius held. ⟦q13.3|23+24⟧ He would not have been seen saying such things — no, countless others — as is clear to the diligent from his writings.

⟦q13.3|25⟧ Whence, then, and from which of the teachers, will they demonstrate that the natures in Christ, from which he also is — preserved after the union, as they say, even by their own account — ought not to be piously confessed by the faithful as two natures? ⟦q13.3|26⟧ For no one at all of the approved teachers is found to have decreed this; on the contrary, all both said it, and taught the faithful through their own words to say it; unless indeed, fashioning from their heart, as is their custom, what seems good to them, they should put forward the fiction as from one of the Fathers, for the deception of the more simple. ⟦q13.3|27⟧ But these men, as it seems, deeming it a shame to be persuaded, and preferring their attachment to the men who deceived them from the beginning [0497] to the divine love, and honouring contentiousness above piety, make the acceptance and honour from God for the concord of the faith lower than being honoured as priests by men — to whom they bring the deception by lying against us of things that are not — and than receiving evil in return for evils, I mean the perishable things as the wage of deception; and they do not cease from warring against the truth and attempting to draw away from it as many as they can.

⟦q13.3|28⟧ Therefore I, the least, exhort you — being genuine children of the holy apostolic Church, in which, illumined through the regeneration of the divine washing, you were deemed worthy to be adopted to God in the Spirit — to withdraw from such men, remembering the holy Apostle Paul writing to the Romans in this manner: I exhort you, brethren, to watch those who make the dissensions and the stumbling-blocks contrary to the teaching which you learned, and turn away from them. ⟦q13.3|29+30⟧ For such men do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own belly; and through fair speech and blessing they deceive the hearts of the innocent. [n: Rom. xvi, 17, 18.] And again, concerning these same men, accustomed to stir up troubles in the Church of God, writing to the Corinthians thus: For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into Apostles of Christ. ⟦q13.3|31⟧ And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. ⟦q13.3|32+33⟧ It is no great thing, then, if his ministers also are transformed as ministers of righteousness; whose end shall be according to their works. ⟦q13.3|39⟧ Remembering these words always, I ask you, blessed ones — I wish you all to hold fast, with all attention and care, to piety, than which nothing is more proper to men for being made friends with God; turning away with all strength from those who do not accept the pious and saving doctrines of the Church; and above all, having learned that it is of the teaching of the Antichrist not to confess in the flesh our Lord

⟦q14.2|1⟧ *A concise exposition of the acceptance of the expressions of the faith that are rightly confessed concerning Christ according to the catholic Church.*

⟦q14.2|2⟧ But we — with God be it said — who feed on the divine and pure pasture of the ecclesiastical teaching, having the glory of piety unassailable, make bold to confess before God and men, piously, all the pious expressions of the Fathers concerning Christ, receiving each with pious intention and fitting reasoning; just as from above and from the beginning, through those who became ministers of grace, we were catechized in the saving word of the faith. ⟦q14.2|2⟧ We confess, then, our Lord Jesus Christ from two natures, as composed of Godhead and manhood; and in two natures, knowing him as being in Godhead and manhood. ⟦q14.2|3⟧ For just as, saying "from two natures", we hold that he is from Godhead and manhood, so also, saying "in two natures", we fittingly signify that he exists in Godhead and manhood; as being separated, after the union, from none of the natures of which he is constituted, but both being and being known in them, from which he also always is. ⟦q14.2|4⟧ And again we confess him two natures united according to hypostasis without division, believing the same to be truly God and man, and that he verifies the names by the very realities. ⟦q14.2|5⟧ For as we believe him both to be and to be called Son of God and God by nature and in truth, because of the identity of essence with the God and Father, so also we say that he both is and is called Son of man, and man become, by nature and in truth, because of the natural kinship according to the flesh with her who bore him. ⟦q14.2|6⟧ For if we do not confess him two natures, as at once God and man, we shall be convicted of saying that he is composed of bare names and not of realities, and is not in truth that which is signified through the names to be. ⟦q14.2|7⟧ So that — by those very men's account — he who chooses to blaspheme could at last suppose, so to say, that what is worshipped and adored by us is nothing: which has passed beyond every excess of impiety.

⟦q14.2|8⟧ Wherefore, guarding ourselves [0501] against being brought under a charge of blasphemy, we do not cease confessing Christ from two natures, as from Godhead, as has been said, and manhood; and in two natures, as in Godhead and manhood; and two natures, as believing the same to be at once God and man; since we know him to be not only from these, but also these; nor these only, but also in these; as a whole from parts, and a whole in parts; and being a whole through the parts. ⟦q14.2|9⟧ For if he who gave being to the things that are also granted them the power for permanence, so that the species should not be commixed with one another nor be converted into one another, but each remain according to the principle by which it has come to be from him — so that, from the stability of the natural property of each, those who love contemplation and are diligent about divine things may conceive, as far as is attainable, the all-wise and knowing Maker and Marshal of the universe — much more would he confirm in himself his own infinitely powerful power: remaining what he was, and becoming what he was not; and not denying what he became, together with remaining what he was, by being both without deficiency and without change.

⟦q14.2|10+11+12⟧ And we say piously also one nature of God the Word incarnate — incarnate in flesh having the intellectual and rational soul — bringing in, by adding "Incarnate", the signification of our essence. ⟦q14.2|10+11+12⟧ For it is a periphrasis that shows in one and the same, by way of union, the two natures, through a name and a definition: through a name, "the one nature of the Word", which signifies the common of the essence together with the proper of the hypostasis; through a definition, the human nature, as the teacher himself says: «For what is the nature of manhood, except that it is flesh intellectually ensouled?» ⟦q14.2|10+11+12⟧ So that he who says "one nature of God the Word incarnate" shows that God the Word is with ensouled flesh, understanding the flesh to be something certainly other according to essence than God the Word — he, at least, who is the true and unadulterated disciple of piety. ⟦q14.2|13⟧ And saying "the union according to hypostasis", we both understand and confess that the union of the natures has come to be into one hypostasis; so that neither is or is understood at all by itself, but with the one compounded and grown together with it; nor again is it commixed with the other according to the essential principle, or has it suffered from the union, in any respect whatever, diminution of its natural perfection. ⟦q14.2|14⟧ And again we confess "the natural union" in the sense of saying "true", just as the holy Cyril himself both said and explained these expressions; and not for the destruction, after the union, of the two natures from which Christ is, or of one of them, as Apollinarius, Eutyches and Severus, following Simon Magus, Valentinus and Manes, have set it forth; as it is easy for those who wish to see, from the writings of Severus himself, through the agreement of the words, the [0504] identity of his doctrines with those of the impious men named.

⟦q14.2|15⟧ Likewise we say that the two births are of the same one Christ: the one from God the Father before the ages, and the one that came to be for us in the last times from the holy Virgin; and likewise we glorify as of the same both the miracles and the passions. ⟦q14.2|16⟧ We confess also the holy all-glorious Virgin properly and in truth Theotokos, as having become mother not of some mere man — even if formed beforehand, as in the twinkling of an eye, apart from the union with the Word, and deified by progress of works and by the summit of virtue — but truly of God the Word himself, the one of the holy Trinity, incarnate from her by an ineffable conception, and perfectly become man.

⟦q14.2|16⟧ These expressions, then, the holy Church of God, having taught her own piously both to say and to understand, has entrusted to be guarded by the divine and bright light of knowledge; exhorting, through both Prophets and Apostles, and through Christ himself, who by his own sufferings fastened her together and fitted her, to take up a life suited and fitting to the great profession of faith: Considering what is the will of God, the good and acceptable and perfect; and keeping watch unto it. ⟦q14.2|17⟧ For we have been taught that we need the best conduct no less than pious faith for attaining everlasting life; lest, building on the foundation of the faith things that do not belong to it, by wicked practices, as having outraged the calling and the grace of the adoption, we make ourselves liable, instead of joy and endless glory, to everlasting fire.

⟦q14.2|18⟧ Seeing, then, many ways of virtues, you blessed ones and sober lovers of the blessed beauty of Christ — ways given to men by the Lord of all, having one goal, and all arriving at one end, unto salvation — let us not neglect our own salvation, nor let slip the time given us for repentance, which it is impossible to attain again. ⟦q14.2|19⟧ But before we go, as the great Job says somewhere, whence we shall not return, to a land dark and gloomy, to a land of everlasting darkness, where there is no light, nor to see the life of mortals, let us be eager to propitiate God, each according to his own power. ⟦q14.2|20⟧ For in view of the variety and difference of the states of our souls, he, as good, has fittingly made many also the ways that lead those who travel by them blamelessly to the everlasting mansions; so that each, choosing the one suited to himself, and running the course of his life by it, may attain the all-glorious place laid up in the heavens according to our hopes.

⟦q14.2|21⟧ Therefore, as we have power, by the co-operation and grace of Christ, let us lay hold of our duties. ⟦q14.2|22⟧ Let us lighten with compassion the misfortune of the poor man, and let us not [0505] neglect to make his want more moderate. ⟦q14.2|23+24+25+26+27+28+29⟧ Let us not put off covering the nakedness of the naked, revering the garment of incorruption given to us. ⟦q14.2|23+24+25+26+27+28+29⟧ Let us suffer with those worn down in the affliction of prison and in weakness of body, and pressed down by the burden of exile, and let us be eager to make the hardships of others our own;
