considering it better and more honourable to hold the last rank with God than to bear the first things of those on earth with the king below: in which, beginning to converse with ourselves, and having accustomed the senses of the soul, quietly, in stillness, to see creation wisely, we shall carry off the greatest gain — to be well guided through the turmoil and instability of visible things to the things that stand and are not moved; and not to remain among them, nor to endure being held fast in them; from which, hating the disorder of the one and longing for the firm footing of the other, we shall call on abyss with abyss; [n: Psal. xli, 8.] perceiving, through the mighty works in visible things, the principles in intelligible things, as far as is attainable to men; and thus, simply, through speechlessness, peering into the inmost sanctuary of the sanctuaries, we shall come to know our own worthlessness, being mystically taught through the oracles of the Spirit how, being earth and ashes, [n: Gen. xviii, 27.] we lay claim to divine glory, by the grace of him who was well pleased; and into what kind of blessedness what is by nature worthless and contemptible is refashioned. ⟦q14.2|23+24+25+26+27+28+29⟧ And thus, struck with amazement at the spectacles of the infinite, we shall gather humility, the strong safeguard of the virtues, God's greatest and first gift, which is the fruit of the true philosophy; through which, mortifying the causes of the passions — I mean the senses — together with the kindred affinity of sensible things toward them, we cut ourselves off from the world altogether, so as to be able to apply ourselves to intelligible things with an undisturbed eye of the soul. ⟦q14.2|23+24+25+26+27+28+29⟧ Out of which, or after which, the divine love, taking over the soul, now truly qualified by humility and henceforth become capable of receiving the image of the divine reflection, makes us friends instead of servants, bestowing the summary of the law, the: Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with [0508] all thy soul, and so on, [n: Matth. xxii, 37.] in permitting none of the intellectual powers in us to reach out at all to anything else than, manfully, to God.

⟦q14.2|23+24+25+26+27+28+29⟧ Let us strive, then, while we have the time set before us by God, [n: Galat. vi, 10.] to bring to work the goal of the pious and Christian profession. ⟦q14.2|23+24+25+26+27+28+29⟧ And since Our wrestling is not against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers, against the world-rulers of the darkness of this age — the unseen tyrants and enemies, who do not join battle in the open, but entwine their wars in the hidden place of the heart — Let us take up the whole armour of God, as the divine Apostle exhorts us, that we may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having accomplished all, to stand; and having girded our loins in truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, in which all the fiery darts of the evil one shall be quenched. [n: Ephes. vi, 12.] Let us persevere in all prayer and supplication, and receive the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, which divides — to put it briefly — the worse from the better, and teaches the pious the conduct fitting for Christians, which is the work of perfect discernment: exactness of the eyes, continence of the tongue, discipline of the body, a lowly mind, purity of thought, the abolition of anger, as the great Basil says somewhere; the mind's flight up to God; and to struggle against temptations for the guarding of precious things; to add more when pressed into service; not to go to law when robbed; to measure out love in return for hatred; to match endurance to persecutions; entreaty to blasphemies; to die to sin; to be crucified with Christ; to transfer love wholly to God, without relation.

⟦q14.2|30⟧ These things I have written, my blessed master, not being ignorant of your firmness of faith in Christ, and the dignity growing in him through the commandments; but wishing you to know of what kind and how great a struggle I have for you, ever burning up my heart with care; and I exhort you to watch the champions of the heresies more soberly, lest any of them, having beguiled you with the persuasive speech of falsehood, should be able to muddy the clear and living stream of the faith in you with the filth proper to the impious doctrines — which may it not be. ⟦q14.2|31⟧ For they possess a tongue that is a two-edged sword and a sharpened razor, slaughtering souls, and sending them on to the trap of Hades and the pit of darkness, and depriving them of the life in Christ through their deluded fair speech. ⟦q14.2|32⟧ But [0509] our Lord and God Jesus Christ himself, the only-begotten Son and Word of God and the Father, the Maker of all creation visible and invisible, who for his unspeakable love for man, as he himself was well pleased, accepted death for us, and rescued us by his own blood from the power of darkness: may he himself hold your right hand, and guide you into his fear, and fill you with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and spiritual understanding; and persuade you to walk worthily of him, bearing fruit in every good work, and growing in the knowledge of his truth; and strengthen you with all power, according to the might of his glory, unto all edification and long-suffering; and, keeping you striving together, with joy and thanksgiving, for the gospel of his grace, deem you worthy of the portion of the saints in light, [n: ibid. 9-12.] by the prayers and supplications of our all-glorious Lady, the Theotokos and ever-virgin Mary, and of all the saints. ⟦q14.2|33⟧ Amen.

⟦q15.1|1⟧ LETTER 13

⟦q15.1|1⟧ *Of the same, to Peter the illustris: a concise discourse against the doctrines of Severus.*

⟦q15.1|2⟧ My blessed master has truly shown that bodily absence from one another can do nothing toward the diminution of spiritual love, for those who are intellectually fitted to one another through love according to God; not having disdained to visit, through his precious syllables, me, the lowly and sinner, who has nothing worthy of his love. ⟦q15.1|3⟧ Which having received, I embraced and greeted them rejoicing, as if he himself were present in the spirit, and gave thanks, as is my custom, to the only God and Saviour of all, Christ, having learned that he had accomplished the watery way in safety. ⟦q15.1|3⟧ For truly sweet is my blessed master when present, and when absent, no less than when present, he is lovable to all, because of the grace of the poverty of the Holy Spirit [n: Matth. v, 3.] that shines upon him; through which everyone who genuinely lays claim to this, as the virtue of God, becomes a holy temple for a dwelling of God in the Spirit — of him who humbled himself unto the form of a servant, and by work and word showed it in himself to men: whom imitating, my blessed master too has inwardly acquired both meekness and humility. ⟦q15.1|4+5+6+7⟧ Meekness, that, quenching the passionate movements of anger and desire, he may become well-pleasing to God and men. ⟦q15.1|4+5+6+7⟧ For meekness is nothing other than [0512] a complete immobility of anger and desire toward what is contrary to nature; by which the divine will becomes manifest to those who have it. ⟦q15.1|4+5+6+7⟧ For the great David, singing psalms, says: He will guide the meek in judgement; he will teach the meek his ways. [n: Psal. xxiv, 9.] And humility, that, cutting out the callosities of pride, he may become both grateful to God and approachable to all men. ⟦q15.1|8⟧ For humility is each one's recognition, by juxtaposition with God side by side, of the transcendent and productive cause; by which the co-disposition of men toward one another naturally comes to be, and the remission of offences is given to those who owe. ⟦q15.1|9⟧ For see, says the same great David again, my humility and my toil, and forgive all my sins. [n: ibid. 18.]

⟦q15.1|10⟧ Being thus, then, in regard to life, my blessed master I pray may be preserved in the firmness of faith in Christ, unshaken as his name declares, and above every heretical billow, as a genuine child of the holy catholic and apostolic Church of God; founded upon the pious confession, against which the wicked mouths of the heretics, opened like the gates of Hades, have no strength at all. ⟦q15.1|11⟧ For concerning the bastards, and those bastardly grafted in from the wild olive into the good olive, I knew, even before you blessed ones wrote, that, according to the prophetic word, As a dog to its own vomit, [n: Prov. xxvi, 11.] they are bound to return — I mean to the stench of the loathsomeness of their faith; as second Simons, and Demases and Hermogeneses, having chosen to prefer falsehood to truth; and, as they think, wronging the heralds of piety in no way by their apostasy, but rather being justly harmed themselves by the deprivation of grace; and not even able to have to their heart's content the present age, for whose sake they departed from the truth, since it is by nature unstable and easily altered, and ever runs past those who think they hold it.

⟦q15.1|11⟧ For truly loathsome and full of stench, and empty of all grace, is every account that does not maintain that the things from which Christ is are preserved according to nature in the one Christ after the ineffable union; but as it were denies the whole economy of God concerning man, and cuts off from the Word of God what was assumed from the immaculate and holy all-glorious Virgin and in truth Theotokos: a rational, ensouled body. ⟦q15.1|12⟧ For truly he cuts it off in fact, even if he seems somehow barely to confess it with the mouth, for the deception of the hearers, and he denies the incarnation altogether, who does not say that after the union the nature of the flesh is, is preserved and is spoken of, united without confusion and without division to God the Word according to hypostasis — on the pretext, forsooth, of reverence, lest he seem to cut the union by the number — clearly denying, after the union, the whole existence itself, to speak properly, of the natures from which [0513] Christ is.

⟦q15.2|1⟧ *A more natural treatment of number.*

⟦q15.2|2⟧ And they suffer this, as it seems, from not knowing that every number, by its own principle, neither divides nor is divided, nor is it at all productive either of division or of union. ⟦q15.2|3⟧ For it is not of a nature to act or to be acted upon, not being an essence or an accident, about which acting and being acted upon are; but only indicative of the quantity of the subject things, however they may happen to be disposed according to relation, whether united or distinguished. ⟦q15.2|4⟧ It is, for instance — if I may make bold to say something — a name of quantity, significative without the relation that attaches to it. ⟦q15.2|5⟧ For neither does number of necessity make the natural distinction of beings, or their quantity; nor does it of itself produce the continuity of things conjoined according to the same species; nor indeed is it universally characteristic of any property of the individuals under the same species that are distinguished from one another by accidents. ⟦q15.2|6⟧ For to do these things is proper to the divine wisdom and power, which constituted the universe and keeps each thing unconfused by the natural boundaries of the beings throughout the universe; but only, as I said, does number make an indication of the quantity of things simply, and not of their how, as a name fitted to quantity.

⟦q15.3|1⟧ *On difference and quantity more exactly, and on their pious confession.*

⟦q15.3|1⟧ If, then, according to the Fathers, number is indicative of the quantity of things but not of their relation; and every quantity contemplated in natural otherness certainly admits difference; and those too who fight against the truth say there is a natural difference in Christ after the union: then they must also say, after the union, the quantity of the things that differ — without which it is impossible for difference to be — together with the number that indicates it, without which it is impossible for quantity to be known at all; if they wish to show the account of their own doctrine coherent according to well-ordered sequence. ⟦q15.3|2⟧ But if they deny the quantity of the natures preserved in Christ after the union, let them not dare to speak even of the difference of the natures from which Christ is after the union; knowing that whatever has difference in any respect whatever cannot be one according to every principle and mode. ⟦q15.3|3⟧ And what cannot be one according to every principle and mode is clearly, according to some principle and mode, two at the least, or more. ⟦q15.3|4⟧ Therefore those who say there is difference in Christ after the union cannot say that Christ is one according to every principle and mode after the union. ⟦q15.3|5⟧ But if Christ is not one according to every principle and mode after the union, clearly, according to some principle and mode, Christ is certainly two after the union. ⟦q15.3|6⟧ And if Christ is two according to some principle and mode after the union, because of the difference in him of the natures from which and in which he is, as the argument has shown, it is clear [0516] that they are impious to no purpose who say the difference of the natures from which Christ is after the union, but plainly destroy by silence, after the union, the natures themselves whose difference it is: for the denial of the things that are and are preserved is truly destruction. ⟦q15.3|7⟧ For either, by their account, the natures have not been destroyed after the union, and they both are and are preserved, and it is just that they be confessed as preserved after the union; or, if it is not just that they be confessed after the union, it is just, by their account, to say that they neither are nor are preserved in Christ, and they have been destroyed. ⟦q15.3|8⟧ For what it is not just at all to name, it is much better, as I think, and more just, to say does not exist at all either. ⟦q15.3|8⟧ Or let them persuade us by argument how it is just that the things from which Christ is, which are and are preserved after the union without any change and alteration whatever, and without conversion into one another according to the essential principle, should not be confessed in Christ; and we readily acquiesce in the privation of the confession of the things preserved and being in Christ.

⟦q15.3|9⟧ And just as Christ is not one according to every principle and mode after the union, so again Christ is not two according to every principle and mode after the union. ⟦q15.3|10⟧ And if Christ is not two according to every principle and mode after the union, then certainly according to some principle and mode — because of the hypostatic identity, that is, the one hypostasis, according to which he cannot have difference — Christ is one. ⟦q15.3|11⟧ Since, then, the same is one and two according to one principle and mode and another, it is necessary to consider according to what principle, and according to what, the same is one and two.

⟦q15.4|1⟧ *That it is blasphemous to say that Christ is simply one nature.*

⟦q15.4|2⟧ If, then, they will say that he is one according to the principle of nature, the whole will clearly, by their account, be one nature simply, without any difference whatever. ⟦q15.4|3⟧ And if we allow them to say this, Christ will be, by their account, neither God nor indeed man, neither creature at all nor Creator. ⟦q15.4|4⟧ For a nature spoken of simply admits, once for all, no signification whatever of either of these. ⟦q15.4|5⟧ But if, fleeing the manifest absurdity, they should say that Christ is one nature, but composite, they have truly not known how the gloom of impiety has thrust them into the last error.

⟦q15.5|1⟧ *On composite nature more exactly, and on the principle of it; and that those who say that Christ is one composite nature are impious.*

⟦q15.5|2⟧ For every composite nature, first, …

⟦q16.1|1⟧ [0517] …has without choice the concourse of its parts with one another in the composition.

⟦q16.1|2⟧ Then, too, it possesses its parts contemporaneous with one another and with itself, co-existing according to their coming-to-be into being, neither part pre-existing the other in time.

⟦q16.1|3⟧ And further still, it is known to have been made for the completion of the totality that magnificently outlines the universe; none of which is at all contemplated in Christ by those who wish to be pious; lest we make the concourse of the Word with the flesh involuntary and without choice; and define either God the Word as contemporaneous with the flesh according to the coming-to-be into being, or the flesh as co-eternal with the Word according to his existence without beginning; or else define Christ as having nothing more than the remaining species contemplated according to universal nature, as brought forth as a part, like the remaining species, for the completion of the universe, by the power that constituted the universe. ⟦q16.1|4+5+6⟧ For this is the definition and principle and law of every composite nature, as the power of truth and the course of logical sequence guide those who make their examination of the things that are with understanding to say. ⟦q16.1|4+5+6⟧ And who will any longer be able to be of the portion of the pious, thinking so about God and Word — him who exists before all the ages; or rather, to speak more properly, the Maker of the ages, who by volition made his self-emptying toward us men voluntary and self-chosen, and became man for the setting-right and renewal, and not for the completion, of the universe? ⟦q16.1|4+5+6⟧ For by a mode of economy, and not by a law of nature, the Word of God ineffably sojourned among men through flesh. ⟦q16.1|7⟧ Christ, then, is not a composite nature, according to the innovation of those who empty the Gospel, being altogether unenslaved to the law of composite nature as to the mode of coming into being; but a composite hypostasis, which has no composite nature whatever predicated of it by species: which is indeed paradoxical, to behold a composite hypostasis without the composite nature predicated of it by species.

⟦q16.1|8⟧ But if, according to those very men, Christ is a composite nature — the wonderful acropolis of Severus's arguments — it is altogether either generic or singular. ⟦q16.1|9⟧ For to conceive another between these is impossible. ⟦q16.1|10⟧ And if Christ is a generic nature, he will clearly be predicated of many things, and of things differing in number; and he will be in thought alone, in those in which he has his existence, and not known by himself in some hypostasis of his own, apart from the accidents contemplated in addition in the individuals under him. ⟦q16.1|11⟧ For such is the definition and principle of every generic nature; and a multitude of Christs has been brought in upon us instead of one, having in no mode any identity whatever with God or with men, through Severus's excessive and unrestrained madness against the truth. ⟦q16.1|12⟧ But if Christ is a singular nature — to pass over saying that there is in no way at all a nature circumscribed by one person, even if they put forward, as a last resort, the fabled bird, [0520] the phoenix, as something great and unassailable, an example establishing their own opinion; against which I am even afraid to say anything, lest among the understanding I incur the laughter that folly earns, trying to show the myth to be a myth. ⟦q16.1|13⟧ For if the phoenix is a bird, it is altogether also an animal. ⟦q16.1|14⟧ And if an animal, first, it is not wholly singular, inasmuch as it is an animal. ⟦q16.1|15+16+17+18⟧ Then, if an animal, it is also an ensouled, sentient body. ⟦q16.1|15+16+17+18⟧ And if the phoenix is an ensouled, sentient body, it is clearly also subject to coming-to-be and corruption. ⟦q16.1|15+16+17+18⟧ Let us ask the wise beholders of the things that are themselves whether it is possible for any of the ensouled and sentient bodies subject to coming-to-be and corruption to be of a nature singular according to hypostasis — bodies whose succession from one another according to species is the conspicuous character and definition of their being. ⟦q16.1|15+16+17+18⟧ As the divine Scripture also testifies, furnishing of itself certainty to the account, when it introduces God commanding these things to the great Noah: And God said to Noah, Enter thou and all thy house into the ark, for I have seen thee righteous before me in this generation. ⟦q16.1|19+20⟧ And of all the clean cattle bring in to thee seven and seven, male and female; and of the cattle that are not clean, two and two, male and female; and of all the clean birds of heaven, seven and seven, male and female, and of all the birds of heaven that are not clean, two and two, male and female, to keep seed alive upon all the earth. [n: Gen. vii, 1-3.] Among which, if the phoenix, as a winged animal, is numbered, it is not of a nature singular according to hypostasis, by the divine declaration. ⟦q16.1|19+20⟧ But, as I said, let us not say these things — for to fight over things not necessary is not dear to us: it is plain to all that, if Christ is a singular nature, he is consubstantial neither with God and Father nor with men. ⟦q16.1|21⟧ For what is wholly singular according to nature is altogether estranged from natural kinship with anything else whatever. ⟦q16.1|22⟧ But if, according to those very men, as the account has shown, Christ is wholly estranged according to nature from all the things that are, we shall urge the new dogmatists themselves to say what he is according to nature, and on what account they worship Christ, who, so far as the premises of their arguments go, is blasphemed by them as being nothing.

⟦q16.1|22⟧ [0521] If, then, a great and fearful danger of necessity follows, according to the force of the account rendered, for those who say that Christ is one according to nature, that is, one nature, whether called simple or composite, and this either generic, that is, common, or singular, that is, specific, let us with all vigilance keep our hearts pure of such an opinion, that we may also be set free from the threat that awaits it. ⟦q16.1|23⟧ And let us piously confess the "two" in Christ according to the principle of natural otherness, that is, of the difference of the natures from which he is, preserved even after the union, as of parts in a whole; according to which the parts never naturally coincide with one another, so long as each keeps unimpaired its own principle of nature relative to the other; and the "one" according to the principle of hypostatic identity, according to which Christ, as a whole, admits no distinction at all from difference with respect to himself, that is, no partition, so long as he is believed to be one hypostasis both before the flesh and after the incarnation, and is worshipped and glorified by us as one of the holy and royal Trinity. ⟦q16.1|24⟧ For Christ's hypostasis is singular, as a whole, divided out to the extremes on no account, according to its characteristic property, by which it is marked off from them. ⟦q16.1|25⟧ By extremes I now mean God and Father, from whom Christ has been begotten divinely before the ages, and the holy, all-glorious Virgin and Mother, from whom the same has been born humanly for our sake — the hypostasis keeping undiminished, by the kinship of its own parts with both the extremes, the identity according to essence; in which parts Christ, admitting the principle of difference, does not depart from his own singular hypostasis. ⟦q16.1|26⟧ For every totality, and especially one by composition, contemplated from different things, while singularly keeping the identity of its own hypostasis, also has the unconfused difference of its own parts with one another, according to which it preserves unadulterated the principle according to essence of each part relative to the other. ⟦q16.1|27⟧ And likewise the parts too, in their composition with one another, keeping pure and undiminished the principle according to nature, have the unitary, undistinguished identity of their own totality, according to which they singularly keep wholly undivided the principle according to hypostasis.

⟦q16.1|27⟧ If, then, as the account, running with truth, has shown, it is altogether impious in Christ to decree that the "one" lies in the principle according to nature, as, conversely, the "two" in the principle according to hypostasis — for the one is proper to the stench of Apollinarius, who smears together and confounds the natures into one nature, and makes the economy wholly indiscernible, positing that properly no nature exists after the union. [0524] For each of these escapes being what it is, as they pass over and fall into one another. ⟦q16.1|28⟧ And the other is proper to the Jewish derangement of Nestorius, who partitions the one hypostasis into two hypostases, and denies the whole economy, refusing to say that God the Word was united to flesh according to hypostasis, essentially. ⟦q16.1|28⟧ We, for our part, let us use our speech rightly and fittingly, turning the expressions of the perverse to what is straight: the "two" according to the principle of natural otherness, that is, of difference; the "one" according to the principle of the hypostasis; that both the differentness of the natures from which Christ is may be kept in Christ after the union, and the sameness and singleness of the hypostasis of God the Word incarnate may likewise be preserved unmultiplied. ⟦q16.1|29⟧ For the reciprocal indication and confession of the realities, as the heretics have it, works the obliteration of the subjects; since the truth does not at all endure to allow the proper appellations of the realities to be exchanged for one another. ⟦q16.1|30⟧ For this reason we confess Christ two natures, as I said, according to the principle of the difference of the natures from which he is, preserved in him even after the union, as being the same God and man after the union.

⟦q16.2|1⟧ *That he who calls Christ God and man after the union, having chosen to believe rightly, of necessity confesses together with the names the natures after the union.*

⟦q16.2|2⟧ For if Christ is God and man after the union, according to the common confession, clearly, having the realities, he makes the names true after the union. ⟦q16.2|3⟧ For realities are conceived before their own names; and there could never at any time be a name without the reality, which of itself provides the name with its imposition and receives in return its signification. ⟦q16.2|4⟧ But if Christ does not have in the union the realities of which the names are, he will be shown, on their account, to have the appellations bare, as lying with nothing, and empty of realities; and Christ will be, according to them, God and man in name only, and not in reality: than which what could be more godless? ⟦q16.2|5⟧ But if, refusing to be so mad, they should say that in Christ the appellations are not empty of realities after the union, then, just as they do not refuse to speak of the two appellations of Christ after the union, so let them also speak, after the union, of the two natures of Christ, from which and in which he subsists, of which the appellations also are — if in truth they faithfully confess that the things united are preserved after the union really, according to nature.

⟦q16.3|1⟧ *On the expression "In two"; and on the one nature of the Word incarnate, a pious confession according to the Fathers; and a denial of the one composite nature.*

⟦q16.3|2⟧ And again we believe the same to be in two natures without division, as in Godhead and manhood. ⟦q16.3|3⟧ For just as, saying that Christ is from two natures, we understand him to be from Godhead and manhood, as a whole from parts, so too, saying "in two natures" after…

⟦q17.1|1⟧ [0525] …the union, we believe him to be in Godhead and manhood, as a whole in parts. ⟦q17.1|2⟧ Now the parts of Christ are his Godhead and his manhood, from which and in which he subsists. ⟦q17.1|3⟧ And again we have been taught to believe, to say and to proclaim one nature of God the Word incarnate, in flesh having an intellectual and rational soul, according to the holy Cyril; understanding, by the saying "incarnate", that the essence of our nature has been brought in. ⟦q17.1|4⟧ And again, of one and the same Christ both the miracles and the passions; and of the same the two births, the one before the ages, bodilessly, from the Father, and the one in time, bodily, from a Mother and Virgin, accomplished for our sake. ⟦q17.1|5⟧ Therefore above all, and in truth, we confess her properly Theotokos, as having given birth to God the Word, begotten of the Father before all the ages, incarnate from her in the last times.

⟦q17.1|6⟧ But we altogether refuse to say that Christ is one composite nature: not only for the reasons stated, but because no one at all of the approved Fathers has appeared up to now to have spoken this expression, and as being manifestly the offspring of Apollinarius the heretic and of his disciples; whose error Severus having accepted, he fittingly also decks himself out in their expressions. ⟦q17.1|7⟧ For Christ is not a natural monad by composition, as Apollinarius and Severus have it, so long as he keeps preserved, even after the union, the unconfused otherness of the natures from which he is. ⟦q17.1|8⟧ Nor yet a hypostatic dyad, as Nestorius has it, so long as the things that came together do not subsist by themselves and wholly distinguished from one another; and so long as God the Word incarnate is one even after the incarnation, and assumed the flesh united to him, rationally and intellectually ensouled, which had not pre-subsisted by the proper principle of its nature; but one composite hypostasis, according to the Fathers, according to which the same is both wholly God, and one of the holy and all-praised Trinity, with the manhood, because of the Godhead; and the same wholly man, and one of men, with the Godhead, because of the manhood.

⟦q17.2|1⟧ *On the composite hypostasis, a more natural treatment; and an exact demonstration that those who confess Christ one composite hypostasis do not fall into the same absurdities as those who call him one composite nature.*

⟦q17.2|2⟧ But if anyone should think that, because every composite hypostasis too possesses its parts contemporaneous with one another, the same absurdity is concluded also for those who say that Christ is one composite hypostasis, such a one, by my account, does not suppose rightly. ⟦q17.2|3⟧ For not simply every composite hypostasis has its parts contemporaneous with one another in coming-to-be, but that which ranks, clearly, under a composite nature, and has such a species predicated of it; which, having [0528] the aggregate of the idioms about it interwoven with the common and universal of the essence or nature predicated of it, is a nature, that is, with idioms. ⟦q17.2|4⟧ If, then, the nature under which it ranks, and the species predicated, is composite, it too must altogether be composite, and possess its parts contemporaneous with one another, because of the essence, that is, the nature, predicated of it, which so exists as to be the same as it in species, apart from its distinguishing marks that mark it off. ⟦q17.2|5⟧ For just as, defining the hypostasis spoken of simply, we say: Hypostasis is an essence with idioms; or, an essence comprehensive of the particulars, of all the idioms in its own individual; so, defining the hypostasis spoken of with a qualification, and not simply, we say: A composite hypostasis is a composite essence with idioms; or, a composite essence comprehensive of the particulars, of all the idioms in its own individual. ⟦q17.2|6⟧ For what is contemplated in common in the individuals under the same species characterizes primarily the generic of the essence or nature in the individuals under it. ⟦q17.2|7⟧ But the composite is common to all the individuals under the composite species; therefore the composite primarily characterizes a composite nature in the individuals under it, and not a hypostasis.

⟦q17.2|8⟧ And again, besides, every definition of the individuals that rank under them is from the common and universal; and all the things under the generic naturally have from them the beginning of their own description, so that it may be clear what the thing defined properly and primarily is. ⟦q17.2|9⟧ But if this is true, as indeed it is, it is plain that he who has called composite a hypostasis referred to a nature has declared, together with the individual of the hypostasis, what inheres generically in the common of the essence, with the idioms that characterize it specifically. ⟦q17.2|10⟧ So that he who has said that a hypostasis ranking under some nature is composite has said nothing other than a composite nature, that is, essence, with idioms. ⟦q17.2|11⟧ If, then, as has been shown, every composite nature has without choice the concourse of its own parts with one another in the composition, and possesses its parts contemporaneous with one another, and has come to be for the completion of the totality contemplated in the things that are, which makes up the universe species by species; then clearly every hypostasis too, according to what is natural, has a constitution unto being the same as, and invariant with, its own genus and species. ⟦q17.2|12⟧ Let them show, then, that Christ's composite hypostasis ranks under a composite nature, and let them conclude that it possesses its parts contemporaneous, and let them justly lay the same blame against us. ⟦q17.2|13⟧ But so long as they cannot do this, they are setting the props of their own doctrines upon sand. ⟦q17.2|14⟧ For he who ignorantly forces Christ under these aforesaid absurdities, because he both is a composite hypostasis and is piously confessed so by us, has wandered far from the road that leads to the truth — or rather, to speak more properly, from the truth itself. ⟦q17.2|15⟧ For this great and venerable mystery of Christ [0529] neither has, as an individual, some universal and generic nature predicated of it as a species; nor indeed is it itself a genus or a species predicated of the individuals naturally under it, so as to be able to be brought under any of the rules stated; inasmuch as it has the concurrence of God the Word with the flesh in the composition not equal and like to that of composite things in their concourse with one another.

⟦q17.3|1⟧ *That only the union of the Word with the flesh has come about by assumption, since he pre-existed and willed to be emptied unto union with flesh.*

⟦q17.3|2+3⟧ For in the case of all things universally that are composite according to nature, it is not the concourse of this with that by assumption that makes the constitution of this species, as of a whole from parts; but the simultaneous coming-to-be of the parts from non-being into being, by their concourse with one another at the same time as their being, makes the composition of the whole. ⟦q17.3|4⟧ But the mystery of our Lord and God and Saviour Jesus Christ did not come about in this mode; but being God by nature, and by nature Son of God, simple and bodiless, and co-eternal with the Father, and Creator of all the ages, willing, by a wish of love for man, he became man by assumption of flesh; and for our sake, being simple according to nature and bodiless, he became from us, by way of economy, composite according to hypostasis and embodied, as the holy and great Dionysius the Areopagite says, under divine inspiration, in the first chapter of his treatise *On the Divine Names*, going through the matter of the divine incarnation thus: « And man-loving pre-eminently, in that it has wholly shared, in truth, in what is ours, in one of its hypostases, calling back to itself and raising up the human extremity, from which [ineffably] the simple Jesus was composed; and the eternal has taken on extension in time; and he has come to be within our nature who superessentially transcends every order according to nature. »

⟦q17.3|4⟧ If, then, not according to the law and order of the nature of composite things, but by another ordinance, contrary to the nature of composite things — for by assumption the Word of God was inexpressibly composed with the flesh, and not by taking being in a coming-to-be together with the flesh unto composition, for the completion of some whole according to species, as the word of truth piercingly cries out to all — then in vain do the ignorant lawlessly attempt to bring under the ordinances that are under nature the composition that goes beyond every definition and principle of nature. ⟦q17.3|5⟧ For this reason he who says that the becoming man came about by assumption of flesh both preserves the existence of God the Word before the ages, and piously confesses his voluntary and self-chosen incarnation in time; and keeps unconfused, even after [0532] the union, the difference between the Word himself who assumed and the flesh assumed. ⟦q17.3|6⟧ But he who does not confess that the Word of God became man without change by assumption of flesh will be able in no mode truly to confess any of the things stated. ⟦q17.3|7+8⟧ For how, if the Word did not pre-exist without beginning, did he by volition assume flesh different according to essence? — in whose case above all, as I think, the union of what is of another nature is properly said to have come about by assumption; since he alone, and alone in this manner, impassibly and truly assumed what is of another essence, and kept himself unchangeable and unmultiplied in every principle and mode, and what was assumed unalterable: which is impossible to come about in the case of originated nature, in which every composition naturally comes about at the same time as the coming-to-be of the parts, for the completion of some whole according to species, by their simultaneous concurrence with one another, keeping equal, throughout the whole, the proportion of the parts to one another; as is the case with us, and with whatever things have had it as their lot to have a composite nature according to species. ⟦q17.3|9⟧ For in us the soul has the natural powers of the body proportioned to its own operations, the body being receptive according to nature because of the soul's simultaneous coming-to-be into being together with the flesh. ⟦q17.3|10+11⟧ But the Word of God, having in no principle or mode the powers of the nature assumed by him proportioned to his own operations according to nature — for what is above nature is not measured by nature, nor is there anything at all among the things that are receptive of him according to nature — therefore, alone of all, by assumption of flesh rationally and intellectually ensouled, willing, he became man ineffably, as being and pre-being and able for all things, having innovated the natures by the mode above nature, that he might save man.

⟦q17.3|12⟧ This faith I have learned, and in it I have been taught, both by our holy and blessed Fathers who have gone before, and by those now living who have been entrusted with the helm of the catholic holy Church of God and steer her rightly to the harbour of the divine will; with which, by their supplications, I shall also depart, leaving the present life, offering to God, in place of every merit, this confession, undefiled and unstained, and higher than every heretical storm. ⟦q17.3|13⟧ For I cannot boast in a life made splendid with works of righteousness, having become throughout all my life here a self-chosen transgressor of the divine laws.

⟦q17.3|14⟧ These things, then, I have written to you, as far as was possible, in summary, my blessed lords, so that you may know, if there is anything useful in what has been written, how you may at least in some measure send away the wolves clothed in the fleece, who terrify with their meaningless barking the divine and gentle sheep of Christ's holy flock, and may not be swept away by the falsehood that maliciously feigns truth. ⟦q17.3|14⟧ But the sayings of the Fathers that plead for the Church's faith I have not yet been able to put into the letter, because of [0533] the great want of books with me. ⟦q17.3|15⟧ For you have there my blessed master, father and teacher, the lord abba Sophronius, truly sober-minded, and a wise advocate of the truth, and an unconquered champion of the divine doctrines, able in deed and word to contend against every heresy, and, with all his other good things, rich in a multitude of divine books, and eagerly enriching those who wish to learn divine things. ⟦q17.3|16⟧ Resorting to him, then, you will receive, I know well, all the right and unstumbling knowledge of the divine and saving doctrines. ⟦q17.3|17⟧ Farewell.

⟦q18.1|1⟧ LETTER 14

⟦q18.1|1⟧ *Of the same, to the same, a dogmatic letter.*

⟦q18.1|2⟧ God, being good according to nature — nothing of what he naturally does is evil. ⟦q18.1|3⟧ But man, becoming good by diligence of inclination, is always shown rejoicing in the things God naturally does. ⟦q18.1|4⟧ For man has no other discernment of his being good than only his co-disposition toward what is done by God. ⟦q18.1|5⟧ For the making of good things is proper to God; to man, the co-disposition toward them. ⟦q18.1|6⟧ For a man's virtue is to show that what has been made by God is cherished by the disposition of his inclination. ⟦q18.1|7⟧ So then, if everything that has God as the cause of its own coming-to-be is good, then good, with reason, and the greatest of goods, is the union of those who stood apart in faith, since it is manifestly the work of God. ⟦q18.1|8⟧ And if this is altogether true, I know that you rejoice, beholding the scattered being gathered into one, being good as you are, through your co-disposition toward what is noble.

⟦q18.1|9⟧ I beg you, then, God-guarded ones, to receive as good men the bearer of this my modest note, the most God-loving deacon, my lord [0536] Cosmas, a man noble and understanding, and adorned with the manners that are according to God, and to enrol him among your own friends; and, if there should be need to lay a request on his behalf before the God-honoured pope, that he may recover his own rank of the diaconate in the Church in which he had been enrolled, not to shrink from it. ⟦q18.1|10⟧ For so genuinely has he accepted the pious account of the divine doctrines of the Church, as even to champion it ardently, and to know this as the definition and ordinance of piety: never to have refused to hold any of the things that Christ is after the inexpressible union, being at once, in the same respect, truly the same God and man. ⟦q18.1|11⟧ For he did not cast off what he was, becoming truly what he was not; for he is unchangeable. ⟦q18.1|12⟧ Nor did he alter what he became, remaining what he was; for he loves man. ⟦q18.1|12⟧ But he is wholly both, naturally, according to hypostasis, as one from both, and through his one self preserving both without change and diminution, as being truly these by union — the union according to hypostasis. ⟦q18.1|13⟧ For the union according to hypostasis, having its contradistinction against division, and not against the natural difference of the things united according to it, makes a complete abolition of the one and works a firm preservation of the other; of which number is the indication. ⟦q18.1|14⟧ Since no one could ever conceive a difference wholly without share in quantity, even were he the wisest in arguments and the hardest to fight.

⟦q18.1|15⟧ For so long as the parts of the whole by composition, from which the whole is constituted, are preserved without confusion, the natural difference to one another of the parts of the whole that are preserved by union is not unknown. ⟦q18.1|16⟧ And so long as the principle of the difference according to essence of the parts remains preserved in the whole, it is impossible that the quantity of the parts of the whole that differ from one another according to essence should be unknown — of which number naturally makes an indication, and not a division; because number is indicative not of the relation of realities, that is, of union or division, but only of quantity simply, and not of quantity in some manner. ⟦q18.1|17⟧ But if number naturally makes an indication of quantity and not of relation, he who piously uses number after the union only for the indication of the difference, preserved in Christ, of the natures from which he is, does not divide the union at all, but knows only that the natures have remained unconfused after the union; from which the one Christ and Lord, and Son and God, exists — incarnate, clearly, and perfectly become man. ⟦q18.1|18⟧ Therefore he also upholds after the union one nature of the Word himself incarnate, in flesh having the intellectual and rational soul, not ignoring the difference, but removing and, as it were, setting outside the division; that at once, through these very expressions, he may drive [0537] the confusion of Apollinarius and the division of Nestorius, evils diametrically opposed, from the divine court, and may become a pure worshipper of the mystery: confessing the same begotten from above, from the Father, before all the ages, and the same born below — by assumption, clearly, of flesh rationally and intellectually ensouled — from his mother, for our sake, in the last times. ⟦q18.1|19⟧ And for this reason believing the holy Virgin to be properly and in truth Theotokos, since, having conceived the Word himself in place of seed, she both carried and bore him, incarnate from her: the same operating the miracles; the same enduring by volition the experience of human sufferings; the same crucified, buried, risen on the third day according to the Scriptures; taken up incarnate into the heavens, from which, without flesh, he came down to us, as he himself knows; he who, as God according to nature, has no passage from places to places. ⟦q18.1|20⟧ For by nature he is infinite, and for this reason in no mode contained by the things that are, as being free of all circumscription; and by nature loving to man, and for this reason enduring by volition our fleshly birth, and becoming containable by what is ours: the same who will come with his own glory to judge living and dead, and to give to each the just distribution of the things prepared according to worth.

⟦q18.1|20⟧ The aforesaid most God-loving lord Cosmas having gladly accepted this confession, I too accepted him rejoicing, and, having come to know his simple disposition according to Christ, I preferred him to my own soul; and on the dogmatic chapters about which he asked, I have given him a concise answer in writing, which it is fitting that you too, God-guarded ones, should take and exercise. ⟦q18.1|21⟧ For you benefit him by your fine exposition of the text, filling up the sense of what was left out through brevity. ⟦q18.1|21⟧ And so much for this.

⟦q18.1|22+23⟧ I remind you, God-guarded ones, to watch and to pray, according to the Lord's command, that we may not be caught in the snares of the temptations that stand around us on every side. [n: Matth. xxvi, 41.] For if we watch and are sober, I know that we guard ourselves against the wiles of the demons; and if we pray, we draw the divine grace to our help, fighting alongside us and showing us victors over every opposing power, [0540] and delivering us from all error and ignorance. ⟦q18.1|22+23⟧ And this above all we ought to do now, when, even without the commandment, nature becomes the teacher of refuge in God, taking distress as its counsellor. ⟦q18.1|24+25+26+27⟧ For what is more distressing than the evils that now encompass the inhabited world? ⟦q18.1|24+25+26+27⟧ What more dreadful to those who perceive what is happening? ⟦q18.1|24+25+26+27⟧ What more pitiable or more fearful to those who suffer? ⟦q18.1|24+25+26+27⟧ To see a nation of the desert and barbarous overrunning another's land as if it were its own; and the gentle commonwealth being consumed by wild and untamed beasts that have only the bare shape of human form; and the Jewish people, rejoicing from of old in the blood of men, and knowing as the only divine good pleasure the murder of the creature; and for this reason raving the more, so as to become more conspicuous in the wealth of wickedness than all those notorious for vice; and thinking to serve God by the things God abhors; the only people of all the peoples on earth most faithless, and for this reason most fit for the reception of the opposing power; going before in procession, in every manner and disposition, of the sojourn of the evil one; and by what it does announcing the coming of the Antichrist, since it failed to know that of him who is truly Saviour; the hostile and lawless, hating man and hating God, and for this reason the more man-hating because God-hating, and permitted to revel in outrages against the saints, since the vengeance is near, that it may be punished the more justly, once its tyranny and insurrection against God have been made perfectly manifest through the facts; the people that is the patron of falsehood, the craftsman of bloodshed and the enemy of truth; the bitter persecutor of my faith, through which the polytheistic error was dissolved and the phalanxes of the demons were driven away. ⟦q18.1|24+25+26+27⟧ Through which All the nations have clapped their hands, according to the prophecy, and shouted to God with a voice of exultation; for the Lord is most high, fearful, a great King over all the earth. ⟦q19.1|1⟧ *Of the same, on common and proper, that is, essence and hypostasis, to Cosmas, the most God-beloved deacon of Alexandria.*
